events.headline: Moody's raises India's FY27 growth forecast to 7% on broad-based momentum

items.title: Moody's raises India's FY27 growth forecast to 7% on broad-based momentum
items.summary: Moody's Ratings on Wednesday said the Indian economy is expected to grow at a higher rate of 7 per cent in the current fiscal, led by broad-based economic momentum and energy supply shock resilience. In its Global Macro Outlook 2027-28, Moody's, however, said that near-term risks to growth persist as household consumption remains vulnerable to "intensifying and broadening price pressures", with headline inflation close to the upper end of the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) 2-6 per cent target range, while a deficient southwest monsoon and strengthening El Nino conditions will weigh on agricultu

events.article_text:
India is also home to the world's largest single-site refining complex, and its large and sophisticated refining capacity has helped limit fuel supply disruptions while supporting its role as a major exporter of refined petroleum products

Moody's Ratings on Wednesday said the Indian economy is expected to grow at a higher rate of 7 per cent in the current fiscal, led by broad-based economic momentum and energy supply shock resilience.

In its Global Macro Outlook 2027-28, Moody's, however, said that near-term risks to growth persist as household consumption remains vulnerable to "intensifying and broadening price pressures", with headline inflation close to the upper end of the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) 2-6 per cent target range, while a deficient southwest monsoon and strengthening El Nino conditions will weigh on agricultural output and rural demand.

"India's broad-based economic momentum and demonstrated resilience to the energy supply shock warrant upward revisions to our 2026-27 growth forecasts to 7 per cent from 6.5 per cent," it said.

Robust consumption, improving investment dynamics and strong macroeconomic fundamentals imply that the economy appears well positioned to sustain growth near 7 per cent over the medium term, Moody's said.

A sustained private investment boom that materially boosts manufacturing, employment and productivity could lift growth rates above Moody's baseline projections.

"With the RBI on track to raise rates further, tighter monetary policy could delay the recovery in private investment," Moody's added.

India has adjusted to the energy price shock better than previously assumed, helped by its ability to diversify crude and gas supplies and buffer consumers from the immediate price impact through state-backed oil marketing companies and tax cuts.

"High frequency indicators, including robust capital goods production and imports, accelerating industrial credit growth and rising capacity utilisation, suggest that India may be at the cusp of a new private capex cycle after several years of corporate and banking- sector balance sheet repair," the US-based agency said.

Broader economic activity also remains solid amid expanding manufacturing and services purchasing manager indexes and double-digit year-on-year growth in goods and services tax revenue, vehicle sales and merchandise exports, it added.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

analysis.tldr: A major rating agency predicts faster economic growth for India, which could mean more jobs and business activity, though high living costs and rising interest rates remain a worry.
the_story: Moody's Ratings raised India's economic growth forecast for the 2026-27 fiscal year to 7 per cent, up from 6.5 per cent previously.
The upgrade is driven by broad-based economic momentum, strong investment dynamics, and resilience against energy supply shocks.
Risks include household consumption staying vulnerable to intensifying price pressures, with inflation near the upper limit of the RBI's 2-6 per cent target range.
Deficient southwest monsoon and strengthening El Nino conditions (weather patterns that can bring poor rains) are noted as threats to agricultural output and rural demand.

Moody's also pointed to high-frequency indicators like robust capital goods production, accelerating industrial credit growth, and rising capacity utilisation pointing toward a private investment boom.
analysis.what_happened: Moody's Ratings upgraded India's growth forecast for the 2026-27 fiscal year to 7% on Wednesday. This happened because of broad economic momentum, strong investment, and how well India handled energy price shocks by diversifying its oil and gas supplies.
analysis.analogy: It is like a runner who was expected to jog steadily, but because their training and gear are so good, experts now expect them to sprint faster, even though they are still worried about a strong headwind.
why_it_matters_india: Moody's raises India's FY27 growth forecast to 7 per cent -> signals strong economic confidence to global investors -> FIIs (foreign institutional investors, big overseas funds) may pour more money into Indian markets.
Private investment and industrial credit growth pick up -> manufacturing and employment expand -> businesses grow and create more jobs for people.

Headline inflation stays close to the upper end of the RBI (Reserve Bank of India, the central bank that regulates banks and interest rates) target range -> cost of living remains high for households.
Deficient monsoon and El Nino conditions weigh on agricultural output -> rural demand weakens and food prices can rise.

impacts.rationale: An upgraded growth forecast boosts investor confidence in Indian companies, which is generally good for the stock market.
Broad price pressures and potential poor monsoon rains could push prices higher, making everyday items costlier for families — a negative for consumers.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: If the RBI raises interest rates to fight inflation, government borrowing costs can rise, which generally leads to costlier loans for regular people.

watch_next: The progress of the southwest monsoon and El Nino conditions
Updates on the Reserve Bank of India's interest rate decisions
analysis.caveats: Growth could slow down if tighter monetary policy or high interest rates delay private investments, or if bad weather severely hurts agricultural output.

items.title: Murphy Oil Draws Boycott Call Over Israeli Gas Licenses

events.article_text:
ASEAN Moves to Build Emergency Oil Reserves Amid Iran Supply Crisis

Gas-fired power projects dominated Germany's…

Pro-Palestinian activists who pressured Eni and Dana Petroleum to quit an Israeli offshore gas venture are now going after Murphy Oil, the Houston-based company that replaced them on Monday. The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement and its partners called on Murphy on Wednesday to give up the six Zone G exploration licenses it holds 50-50 with Israel’s Ratio Energies. The licenses cover about 1,700 square kilometers of seabed near the Leviathan gas field, and Murphy is the operator.

Israel awarded Zone G in October 2023 to Eni, Ratio and Aberdeen-based Dana, a subsidiary of state-run Korea National Oil Corporation. Eni withdrew earlier this year, citing a reallocation of investments, and Israeli financial daily Globes reported that pro-Palestinian pressure also made the company reluctant to enter Israel.

Israel’s Energy Ministry announced Dana’s exit on Monday, according to Korea’s Yonhap news agency. Dana had faced protests in Aberdeen and a complaint to South Korea’s Board of Audit and Inspection. According to the civic group that filed the complaint, the board closed the case after finding that the licensing process had stopped and that Dana plans to withdraw. Dana and KNOC have not commented. Israeli media have reported that Dana can rejoin with regulatory approval.

Campaigners in Scotland, South Korea and Italy claimed both exits as wins and urged investors, insurers and contractors to stay out of the project. They argue that part of Zone G overlaps the maritime boundaries Palestine declared in 2019, which Israel does not recognize. They also cite a July 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that found Israel’s exploitation of natural resources in the occupied territories unlawful. “Murphy Oil, which has now taken the place Dana and Eni abandoned, should expect exactly the same treatment,” said Dave Black of the Scottish Palestine Solidarity Campaign.

Murphy has not responded publicly to the campaign. On Wednesday, it announced four production sharing contracts covering about 2.6 million acres offshore Cameroon. Murphy and Ratio have 36 months to drill an exploration well in Zone G. Ratio also holds 15% of Leviathan, which supplies Egypt under a $35 billion export contract.

Murphy Oil recently took over a 50-50 partnership with Israel's Ratio Energies after previous partners Eni and Dana Petroleum withdrew following activist pressure.
Campaigners argue that part of the Zone G area overlaps maritime boundaries declared by Palestine, citing a July 2024 International Court of Justice opinion on natural resources.
Murphy and Ratio have 36 months to drill an exploration well in Zone G, while Murphy also recently announced new offshore production contracts in Cameroon.

analysis.analogy: It is like a group of local neighborhood shopkeepers protesting against a major new supplier moving into a disputed marketplace, causing other suppliers to back out and leaving the new company to face all the pressure alone.
why_it_matters_india: Geopolitical friction and activist pressures target energy companies operating in the Middle East.
Global energy exploration shifts can create uncertainty in international fuel and gas markets.
Changes in international energy supply dynamics feed into global crude oil price movements.
For India, an energy-importing nation, shifts in global oil and gas supply stability influence domestic import bills and inflation.

impacts.rationale: While this specific company dispute is localized, broader Middle East energy tensions can push oil prices up, making fuel more expensive for Indian consumers.
Costlier global energy imports increase India's demand for US dollars to pay for oil, which can weaken the rupee and make imported goods pricier for regular people.

events.headline: Off-budget state borrowing: India must treat the illness rather than the symptom

items.title: Off-budget state borrowing: India must treat the illness rather than the symptom
items.summary: Policymakers should reform the rule that caps states' fiscal deficit at 3% of GDP. Trying to bring the hidden debts of states onto the books is laudable but does not suffice. A fiscal architecture designed for a 2003 crisis cannot finance India's ambitions for 2047.

events.article_text:
Few numbers in Indian public finance mislead as much as a state’s reported debt. Behind it sits off-budget borrowing: loans raised outside the Consolidated Fund by state-controlled entities and special purpose vehicles, whose repayment the state ultimately bears, services or guarantees. It has become the headache of Indian fiscal federalism.

The 16th Finance Commission wants off-budget borrowing discontinued and all such liabilities brought onto state budgets, with enhanced disclosure and audit; the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) is holding a national consultation on reporting them.

The mandate deserves support: the Commission’s projected fall in combined Centre-state debt, from 77.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2026-27 to 73.1% by 2030-31, is credible only if hidden liabilities are captured. But it treats the symptom.

If off-budget borrowing is the headache, the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) framework, and its uniform 3% of GDP deficit ceiling, is the tumour beneath.

How large is the problem? The scale is uncertain, which is itself the diagnosis. World Bank estimates put outstanding off-budget borrowing in 2023-24 at ₹1.40 trillion in Andhra Pradesh (11% of gross state domestic product, or GSDP) and ₹1.21 trillion in Telangana (9%). Kerala’s stock was about 3%, though its fresh borrowing that year was the highest among the states covered. Guarantees across 27 states stood at 3.9% of GSDP in 2022-23, 44% of it in the power sector.

Reported figures swing wildly. Punjab’s stock fell from ₹10,551 crore to ₹770 crore in a year; Tamil Nadu’s from ₹27,670 crore to ₹2,299 crore, reflecting reclassification more than repayment. Adding off-budget borrowing and guarantees raises Kerala’s “extended debt” by eight to nine percentage points of GSDP. Yet, hardly any study exists of what the off-budget borrowing of the Union and states has cost us.

A rule its author could not follow: Why do states borrow off the books? The conventional answer is indiscipline; a better one begins with the rule. The FRBM Act of 2003 required the Union to cut its fiscal deficit to 3% of GDP and eliminate the revenue deficit. In 24 budgets since, it has met neither target: the deficit exceeded 3% in 23 years, and the revenue deficit never vanished.

The exception, 2007-08 (2.5%), was itself an off-budget artefact: oil and fertilizer bonds worth about ₹47,757 crore, roughly 1% of GDP, were issued in lieu of cash subsidies. Food subsidy arrears were long parked with the Food Corporation of India. The Act was amended thrice, the Union got a glide path, and from 2026-27, it has effectively moved to a debt anchor of 50% of GDP (with permissible variation of 1% on either side) by 2030-31.

States remain bound by a 3% ceiling, enforced through Article 293(3), with no comparable escape clause, although the case for a debt anchor is stronger for states, which cannot monetize deficits and control barely half their revenues.

The tyranny of the 3% rule: Guy Abeille, a French budget official, recalls devising it in 1981 “on the corner of a table,” in about an hour. It entered the Maastricht Treaty to protect a common currency among mature economies; India adopted it in 2003, justified by household financial savings of about 10% of GDP, now around 5-6%. The premise has eroded; the number survives.

For states, the rule has three fault lines. It targets the deficit’s size, not its use; borrowing for a university and for arrears are treated alike. It imposes a sovereign’s rule on entities of vastly different capacity: own revenue ranges from under 10% of receipts in Manipur to over 80% in Telangana. And it books education, research and health as revenue spending, though the System of National Accounts 2008 treats research and development (R&D) as capital formation.

With committed expenditure absorbing over 70% of own revenue (as in Kerala) and a Union-set cap, a state can forgo investment, breach the rule, or borrow outside the measured perimeter. Only the last satisfies both the rule and the mandate. Off-budget borrowing is less a governance failure than a predictable response to a mis-specified rule: India’s version of Europe’s “creative accounting.”

What should be done: The CAG should build three layers of disclosure.

First, a perimeter test: if the state controls the entity, stands behind its repayment and a default would fall on the Consolidated Fund, the liability is public debt, with self-servicing borrowing distinguished from deficit financing.

Second, an Annual Off-Budget Liability Statement with every state budget, covering interest, maturity, repayment source and use of funds.

Third, verification: concurrent audit of each state’s five largest off-budget entities, reconciliation with lenders’ records, and a National Off-Budget Liability Register covering the Union’s extra-budgetary resources too.

Disclosure alone will not hold. The 17th Finance Commission’s terms of reference should provide for an extended golden rule with a debt anchor; borrowing limits differentiated by revenue autonomy and debt dynamics; capital treatment for knowledge investments; rule-based escape clauses for states; and an independent fiscal council for both tiers.

Systematic study of the costs of off-budget borrowing, and of the investment lost without it, should begin now, rooted in Indian realities rather than borrowed textbooks.

None of this is a licence for laxity; every liability should be counted. But a fiscal architecture designed for the crisis of 2003 cannot finance the ambitions of 2047. The perimeter must be defined before the rule can constrain, and the rule reformed before the perimeter can hold.

The authors are, respectively, director, Gulati Institute of Finance and Taxation (GIFT), and assistant professor, GIFT.

the_story: States engage in off-budget borrowing through loans raised outside official state funds by special purpose vehicles, with repayments ultimately borne or guaranteed by the state.

The 16th Finance Commission wants off-budget borrowing stopped and all such liabilities brought onto state budgets, and the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) is holding a national consultation on reporting them.

World Bank estimates put outstanding off-budget borrowing in 2023-24 at ₹1.40 trillion in Andhra Pradesh (11% of gross state domestic product) and ₹1.21 trillion in Telangana (9%), with Kerala's stock at about 3%.
The author argues that strict rules like the 3% fiscal deficit ceiling force states to hide borrowing, and recommends a debt anchor and tailored rules instead.
analysis.what_happened: Financial authorities like the 16th Finance Commission and the CAG are pushing to uncover hidden government debt because states have been taking loans outside official budgets to bypass strict borrowing limits.
analysis.analogy: It is like a family trying to hide a massive credit card bill by taking loans from relatives, making their household budget look healthier than it actually is.

Hidden liabilities get added to official state debt registers ->

Changes in government borrowing patterns influence overall bond market stability and interest rates.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: If hidden state debts are officially added to public ledgers, overall debt supply increases, which can push yields higher and make government borrowing costlier.

analysis.caveats: The actual timeline and enforcement of the proposed accounting changes depend entirely on future policy adoptions by finance commissions and central authorities.

items.title: Cabinet approves ₹62,370-crore fertiliser subsidy for Rabi season
items.summary: The package includes Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) rates for phosphatic and potassic (P&K) fertilisers for the period October 1, 2026, to March 31, 2027.

events.article_text:
The government had, in fact, cut fertilizer subsidy by over 8 per cent in FY27 from ₹1.86 lakh crore in FY26.

The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved a ₹62,370.02 crore subsidy for different types of fertilizers for the 2026-27 Rabi season, which is ₹24,417.73 crore more than ₹37,952 crore budgeted for 2025-26 Rabi season. With ₹41,533.81 crore subsidy allocated for Kharif 2026, the total outgo and P & K subsidy in FY27 has exceeded ₹1 lakh crore mark, as against budgetary allocation of ₹54,000 crore.

As the government had budgeted ₹1.71 lakh crore total fertilizer subsidy including ₹1.17 lakh crore on urea for FY27, the overall outgo may top ₹3 lakh crore as global prices of both urea and LNG (key input for manufacturing) had also shot up after the Iran war and continued for a longer period.

Total spending on fertilizer subsidy in six months till September has already crossed 70 per cent of the FY27 budget estimates, according to Controller General of Accounts (CGA). It is estimated that total spending for FY27 could touch as high as ₹3.50 lakh crore. When the budget for fertilizer subsidy was lowered, it was said that there would be “reduced requirement for imported urea and P&K fertilizers leading to balanced use of fertilizer nutrients for better soil health and productivity.”

“The higher subsidy bill was expected given global developments on gas in particular. With food inflation rising sharply it is essential to check input costs like fertilizers. It is against this background we should look at higher subsidies. We believe fiscal deficit ratio will be higher up to 0.3 per cent if GDP and this increase has already been factored,” said Madan Sabnavis, Chief Economist, Bank of Baroda.

After the Union Cabinet approval for rabi season (from October 2026 to March 2027), the subsidy on nitrogen (N) will be ₹94.21 per kg against ₹47.32 per kg in kharif 2026 (April-September). Sulphur (S) subsidy has been raised to ₹10.42 per kg from ₹3.16 per kg and phosphorus to ₹66.11 per kg from ₹52.76 per kg. However, potash (K) subsidy has been constant at ₹2.38 per kg for the last few seasons.

Highlighting the increase in subsidy, which is paid to fertilizer companies to make available the crop nutrients at cheaper rates to farmers and keep costs of production under check, the government said that it was necessitated in view of recent trends in the international prices of fertilizers and inputs.

The enhanced outlay comes against the backdrop of global fertilizer price volatility and disruptions arising from the West Asia crisis. The government said the package would ensure adequate availability of fertilizers during the rabi season, while keeping input costs stable for farmers.

Briefing media after the Cabinet meeting, Information and Broadcasting Minister Ashwani Vaishnaw said that the government has also approved a sulphur package for domestic manufacturers. Under this, manufacturers will receive 20 per cent of the actual procurement cost of sulphur and sulphuric acid. However, a floor price of $800 per tonne for sulphur and $266.67 per tonne for sulphuric acid have been fixed.

Stating that detailed guidelines will be issued by the Department of Fertilizers, he said the decision will help strengthen domestic production and reduce import dependence. Besides, it will promote the use of alternatives such as SSP in place of DAP and ammonium sulphate in place of urea, thereby encouraging balanced nutrient application.

The country’s total fertilizer stocks stood at 235.21 lakh tonnes (lt) as on November 10, 2026, against 173.46 lt on the corresponding date last year. Urea stocks were at 103.12 lt against 72.14 lt while DAP stocks rose to 28.65 lt from 24.86 lt. The complex fertilizers (combination of NPKS nutrients) stocks are also higher at 60.87 lt from 42.44 lt and those of MOP are nearly doubled to 20.08 lt from 10.78 lt. Only SSP stocks, were marginally lower at 22.49 lt against 23.24 lt.

Based on the feedback received from States, the Centre has estimated the fertilizer demand in current rabi season at about 350 lt – Urea 199.27 lt, DAP 55.07 lt, MOP 16.4 lt and Complex 79.12 lt.

“Announcing the NBS subsidy well ahead of sowing helps companies to plan import and supply DAP, MOP, SSP and Complex fertilizers in time as it removes uncertainty, though the government keeps assuring to bear the difference between actual cost and its intended selling prices,” said a CEO of a fertilizer company.

Though as per policy fertilizer companies are independent to fix the retail price of DAP, the government has been insisting them not to sell the 50-Kg bag above ₹1,350 and accordingly the subsidy on ‘P’, the main component of DAP, has been revised each season as per global prices.

The government will continue special provisions beyond the NBS framework to ensure DAP is available at ₹1,350 per bag and these provisions have also been extended to imported and domestic TSP and imported MAP.

The freight subsidy on SSP and the subsidy on imported and domestic ammonium sulphate will also continue during the Rabi season.

Describing the Cabinet approval as timely and positive, S Sankarasubramanian, Chairman, Fertilizer Association of India (FAI), said: “The enhanced support will help ensure adequate availability of P&K fertilizers at affordable prices, promote balanced plant nutrition and provide an important impetus to domestic production.”

analysis.tldr: The government is spending much more to help farmers buy cheap fertilisers, which keeps crop costs low but widens the government's budget deficit.
the_story: The Union Cabinet approved a ₹62,370.02 crore subsidy for different types of fertilizers for the 2026-27 Rabi season, which is ₹24,417.73 crore more than the previous year.

Global prices for urea and LNG (liquefied natural gas [gas cooled into liquid for easy transport]) shot up after the Iran war, pushing total annual fertilizer spending towards an estimated ₹3.50 lakh crore.
The subsidy per kg for nitrogen has been raised to ₹94.21, sulphur to ₹10.42, and phosphorus to ₹66.11, while potash remains steady at ₹2.38.
The government also approved a sulphur package for domestic manufacturers, offering 20 percent of procurement costs with fixed floor prices to boost local production.
Total country fertilizer stocks stand at 235.21 lakh tonnes as of November 10, 2026, which is higher than the 173.46 lakh tonnes recorded on the same date last year.
analysis.what_happened: The Union Cabinet approved a massive increase in fertilizer subsidies for the upcoming Rabi (winter-sown) season. This happened because global prices for fertilizers and natural gas surged following the Iran war, forcing the government to step in with more financial support so farmers can continue buying crop nutrients at affordable rates.
analysis.analogy: It is like a grocery store owner absorbing rising wholesale food prices out of their own pocket so regular customers can keep buying milk at the same old price.
why_it_matters_india: Global disruptions push up the cost of making and importing fertilizers.
The government increases payouts to fertilizer companies so they can keep selling bags to farmers at controlled prices like ₹1,350.
Farmers' input costs stay stable, which helps keep food inflation from jumping higher.

Higher government spending widens the fiscal deficit (the gap between government earnings and spending), which can nudge up government borrowing and bond yields (the interest rate the government pays to borrow).

impacts.rationale: Higher subsidies and manufacturing support packages clear uncertainty and secure timely payments for makers, which is generally good for their business.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: A higher government subsidy bill can widen the fiscal deficit, meaning the government borrows more, pushing up yields — generally bad as it raises borrowing costs for everyone.
Keeping farm input costs stable prevents food prices from spiking, which is good for household budgets.

watch_next: Actual total government spending figures at the end of the fiscal year
Global natural gas and fertilizer price trends
analysis.caveats: If global energy prices drop faster than expected, the government's final subsidy payout might not reach the peak estimate of ₹3.50 lakh crore.

events.headline: Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families

items.title: Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families
items.summary: Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families

events.article_text:
An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve Board on Friday released the results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families.

The data provide a representative picture of what Americans own, how and how much they borrow, and how they bank. The current version of the survey has been undertaken every three years since 1989 and provides the public with an extensive time series of thorough information on the economic conditions of American families. Alongside the survey data, the Board issued its summary report entitled Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 (PDF), which examines changes in income, net worth, assets, debt, and financial vulnerability.

In addition to the summary report, an interactive chartbook displaying changes in these financial characteristics over time is available here. Additional data from the survey, including extensive data examining other economic conditions of American families, is made available to researchers and the public here.

The survey is conducted for the Board by NORC, a social science research organization at the University of Chicago. Participants in the study are chosen at random from 119 geographic areas, including metropolitan areas and rural counties across the United States, using scientific sampling procedures that aim to produce a sample representative of American families.

For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call (202) 452-2955.

Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 Evidence from the Survey of Consumer Finances (PDF)

analysis.tldr: A U.S. government survey on American family finances gives hints about the health of the U.S. economy, which can indirectly sway global markets and foreign investments in India.
the_story: The U.S. Federal Reserve Board (the U.S. central bank) released the results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances on Friday.
The survey, conducted every three years since 1989 by NORC at the University of Chicago, details what Americans own, borrow, and how they bank.
Alongside the raw data, the Fed released a summary report called Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 covering income, net worth, assets, and debt.
analysis.what_happened: The U.S. Federal Reserve published a major study tracking the financial health, debts, and savings of American families from 2022 to 2025. This research is gathered by randomly selecting participants across 119 U.S. urban and rural areas to help policymakers understand consumer behavior.
analysis.analogy: It is like a national health check-up for families, helping doctors see if households are getting stronger or weaker over the years.
why_it_matters_india: The U.S. Federal Reserve uses data like this to judge the health of American consumers.
If American consumers are struggling or spending too much, the Fed changes its interest rate policies.
Changes in U.S. interest rates affect how easily FIIs (big foreign investors) move money around the world.
If foreign investors pull money out of emerging markets like India to chase higher returns in the U.S., it can put pressure on Indian financial markets.

impacts.rationale: If the U.S. report shows weak American consumer spending that rattles global markets, foreign investors might pull cash out of Indian stocks, which hurts domestic share prices.
If U.S. economic data makes global investors run toward safer American assets, the dollar strengthens and the rupee weakens, making imported goods like crude oil costlier for India.

watch_next: How global stock markets react to overall U.S. economic health reports
Statements from the U.S. Federal Reserve on future interest rate decisions based on consumer data
analysis.caveats: This survey provides general background economic data rather than an immediate economic shock, meaning its direct impact on India is very slow and indirect.

events.headline: Australia talks tough on Sudan but won’t confront patrons in UAE

items.title: Australia talks tough on Sudan but won’t confront patrons in UAE
items.summary: A risk-averse approach to sanctions means Canberra is only going after those inside Sudan responsible for atrocities.

events.article_text:
Foreign Minister Penny Wong at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, 24 September 2026. She has since announced sanctions on four Sudanese individuals and an armed group over the Sudan conflict. (Miguel Gallagher/DFAT)

A risk-averse approach to sanctions means Canberra is only going after those inside Sudan responsible for atrocities.

Australia talks tough on Sudan but won’t confront patrons in UAE

Australia’s (Opens in new window) response to human rights abuses and foreign policy crises is rhetorically strong but risk-averse. Condemnation and sanctions are a good starting point, but more is needed to curb atrocities such as those taking place in Sudan (Opens in new window).

On 5 November, Foreign Minister Penny Wong announced human rights sanctions (Opens in new window) on four Sudanese individuals and financial sanctions on an armed group in response to the ongoing conflict. This was a positive development, and comes on the back of A$67 million in much-needed humanitarian assistance which Australia has given to Sudan since 2023.

But if Australia is going to have meaningful impact on the abuses, it needs to be willing to take stronger actions against all those implicated in the atrocities, both inside and outside Sudan.

Among those sanctioned was Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as “Hemedti”, commander of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which is fighting Sudan’s military for control of the country. The only other governments to have sanctioned him so far are Canada, and the United States, under President Joe Biden (Opens in new window).

Sanctioning Sudanese commanders is essential, but it is the least we should expect.

Hemedti’s fighters have been responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity since the war started in 2023, including egregious crimes in Darfur last year. For 18 months they laid siege to the city of El-Fasher, forcing starving residents to survive on animal feed until even that ran out. During the last days of the offensive in October 2025, the RSF committed multiple massacres (Opens in new window). The UN Human Rights Office estimated (Opens in new window) that over 6,000 people were killed in just three days, and the UN Fact-Finding Mission on Sudan concluded that the campaign bore the “hallmarks of genocide (Opens in new window)”.

RSF fighters also committed widespread sexual violence against women and girls and ran a large-scale abduction-for-ransom operation, killing those who could not pay. In the siege’s final weeks, their drone attacks targeted not only government soldiers and aligned armed groups, but also killed and maimed civilians trapped in a tiny area.

One of the additionally shocking elements to the RSF conduct is that the United Arab Emirates has continued to provide substantial support to the group despite their well-documented crimes. The UAE has provided the RSF with weapons, supplies, and facilitated the hiring of private military contractors. Colombian operatives trained at UAE military bases were deployed (Opens in new window)alongside the RSF on the front lines of El-Fasher, operating drones and artillery. Survivors’ accounts confirm that the contractors were present during some of the worst atrocities.

The UN Fact Finding Mission has confirmed that individuals and entities with links to the UAE “played a significant role in the recruitment, financing, transportation and deployment of foreign military contractors and the provision of military-related support benefiting the Rapid Support Forces.” In aresolution adopted in July 2026 (Opens in new window), the European Parliament criticised the UAE’s support. It called for sanctions on a UAE company involved in recruiting and transferring mercenaries (Opens in new window) to the group.

The UAE-based Global Security Services Group, which apparently hired the Colombian fighters, has not been sanctioned. Nor is the UAE being held accountable for its military support to the RSF.

The Australian government should be bolder. The UAE is Australia’s largest trading partner (Opens in new window) in the Middle East. Australia should use that leverage rather than remain silent on UAE support for forces committing war crimes. It should publicly call on UAE authorities to immediately stop providing personnel, arms, related equipment, and assistance to the RSF in violation of the UN arms embargo on Darfur.

Australian authorities should also investigate the role, if any, of the Abu Dhabi-based company, its CEO, and other individuals and entities engaging private military contractors to support RSF operations in Darfur. These investigations should examine possible violations of the UN Security Council arms embargo, with a view to imposing additional sanctions.

According to reporting (Opens in new window) at the end of 2025, Australian companies had exported nearly $300 million in arms and ammunition to the UAE over a five-year period. Australia’s legislation contains no end-use monitoring requirements, so there is no legal obligation to ensure that those weapons do not end up in Sudan.

Given the serious risk that Australian weaponry may be diverted to the RSF, Australia should suspend transfers of military equipment to the UAE, including arms, training, and maintenance.

The real test of Australia’s commitment to human rights and opposition to war crimes, crimes against humanity, and other atrocity crimes, is whether it will take uncomfortable measures against more formidable actors – including the UAE. The UAE has ample reason to reconsider its support to the RSF if Australia makes clear that it matters.

Daniela Gavshon is Australia director at Human Rights Watch.

Analysis by Lydia Khalil, Peter Woodrow + 2 others

The most-pressing world events explained by Lowy Institute experts and global contributors, in your inbox, every Thursday.

analysis.tldr: Australia's reluctance to penalize the United Arab Emirates over its involvement in the Sudan conflict leaves global trade and diplomatic ties unchanged for now, having no direct impact on Indian household costs or markets.
the_story: On November 5, Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong announced human rights sanctions on four Sudanese individuals and an armed group over the ongoing Sudan conflict.
The sanctions target Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo ('Hemedti'), commander of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has committed widespread atrocities and war crimes.
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has continued to provide substantial support to the RSF, including weapons, supplies, and the deployment of foreign military contractors trained in the UAE.
The article argues that Australia refuses to confront its largest trading partner in the Middle East, the UAE, and continues its own arms exports to the UAE without end-use monitoring requirements.
analysis.what_happened: Australia has chosen to apply sanctions only against specific individuals and groups directly fighting inside Sudan. It has avoided taking action against external backers like the United Arab Emirates, despite evidence that the UAE has supported the violent paramilitary forces in Sudan, because the UAE is Australia's largest trading partner in the Middle East.
analysis.analogy: It is like a school punishing the local bullies who throw punches, but refusing to speak to the rich kid who buys them their weapons and pays their way, just because that rich kid is the school shop's biggest customer.
why_it_matters_india: Australia limits its diplomatic criticism and sanctions to local actors inside Sudan rather than targeting external economic partners like the UAE.
This political and diplomatic disagreement remains contained entirely between Western nations, human rights groups, and Middle Eastern countries.
Because the event involves no changes to global oil supplies, trade routes, or financial regulations affecting Asia, it does not trigger any transmission mechanism to India.
Consequently, Indian consumer prices, stock markets, and currency values remain unaffected by this diplomatic debate.

impacts.rationale: No direct link exists between Australian foreign policy debates on Sudan and Indian corporate earnings, keeping market movement negligible.
Foreign exchange rates are driven by global capital flows and trade balances, which are completely undisturbed by this political commentary.

watch_next: Whether other major nations decide to follow Australia's lead and investigate external backers of the Sudan conflict
Any future changes to Australian arms export rules and monitoring requirements
analysis.caveats: This analysis relies purely on the provided text, which focuses on diplomatic choices rather than economic disruptions.

events.headline: The Download: Pelosi’s successor targets AI and data centers face power woes

items.title: The Download: Pelosi’s successor targets AI and data centers face power woes
items.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI —Grace Huckins As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a…

events.article_text:
As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.

“We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI. Here’s what he plans to do about it.

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash sweeping the country arguably first began to take shape.

Big Tech has framed the data center uproar as a culture war over progress. But a few days in Ashburn convinced me the real fault line may be electricity: drawing it from the grid or generating it onsite provokes different forms of blowback.

The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Find out why.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 The FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair But Trump says he doesn’t think Huang needs to worry. (AP News) + Huang hired a PR firm known for handling sex scandals last year. (Wired $) + The allegations will likely spur new chip export restrictions. (Reuters $) + They also raise questions about Huang’s lobbying on China. (Verge) + And threaten the fate of the economy. (WP $)

2 France has accused Iran of hacking its supermarket fridges Prosecutors are investigating the leaders of an Iranian cyber unit. (NPR) + Hackers are shifting to manipulating physical equipment. (Axios) + Is your smart kitchen next? (Wired $)

3 The Iran war has triggered a drop in global emissions The main driver is energy supply constraints. (New Scientist $) + But the decline will likely prove temporary. (Gizmodo) + Our climate models have a big blind spot. (MIT Technology Review)

4 The FDA has ordered GLP-1s to carry warnings about blindness It says the drugs may increase the risk of vision loss. (NBC News) + GLP-1s could also exacerbate eating disorders. (MIT Technology Review)

5 Australia is mulling criminal penalties for rogue AI The proposals follow an AI agent hacking government systems. (BBC)

6 The Pentagon is planning to patrol the Moon The project’s first five satellites could launch in 2029. (Ars Technica)

7 Two US cities have voted to ditch Flock surveillance cameras York, Maine, and League City, Texas, have voted to ban them. (Vox) + What Flock’s defenders are missing. (MIT Technology Review)

8 Constant surveillance is changing how children grow up Tracking apps can fuel anxiety and undermine resilience. (Atlantic $)

9 A tiny RNA molecule could explain how life began Some researchers believe life emerged from self-copying molecules. (Quanta)

10 A sci-fi novel has won the Booker Prize for the first time The End of Everything was awarded the prestigious honor. (Gizmodo)

—Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at ​Bernstein, tells Reuters why it will be so difficult to replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO.

Just a short ferry ride from the Chinese port city of Yantai sits Genghai No. 1, a strange offshore complex that combines a tourist attraction with an industrial fish farm. It even has a seven-story visitor center shaped like a cartoon starfish. But its main purpose is to breed fish and release them into the ocean.

Genghai is part of China's ambitious marine ranching program. Since 2015, the country has built 169 demonstration ranches and released at least 167 billion juvenile fish and shellfish. But the approach has also proved controversial.

analysis.tldr: Tighter global rules on artificial intelligence and surging electricity demands from tech hubs could ripple into shifting tech costs and tighter chip exports for India's digital economy.
the_story: Scott Wiener, former California state senator who authored AI risk legislation, won a congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s San Francisco seat and aims to set federal AI policy.
Ashburn, Virginia, known as Data Center Alley and the world's largest data center hub, is facing local backlash driven heavily by enormous electricity grid demands.
The FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair, raising questions about China lobbying and potential new chip export restrictions.
Other global tech developments include France accusing Iran of hacking supermarket refrigerators, and Australia mulling criminal penalties for rogue AI after an AI agent hacked government systems.
analysis.what_happened: US politicians and regulators are pushing back against the rapid expansion and risks of advanced technology. Newly elected US lawmakers are targeting AI safety regulations, while massive data centers are facing local power grid strains, and scrutiny surrounds major tech leadership like Nvidia's CEO.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local electricity grid straining because too many factories opened up at once, forcing the town council to rethink who gets power and how strictly the factories must be monitored.
why_it_matters_india: US politicians push for tighter AI rules and chip export restrictions -> global tech firms like Nvidia face hurdles -> availability and cost of advanced computing hardware for Indian tech companies and startups could shift.

Data centers in major global hubs face acute electricity and power grid constraints -> tech infrastructure growth strains local resources -> multinational tech giants may alter how and where they expand power-heavy infrastructure like server farms.

impacts.rationale: Stricter global AI regulations and hardware export restrictions could slow down global tech spending, which is generally bad for the stock values of Indian outsourcing giants.

watch_next: New US federal AI policy developments under incoming lawmakers
Updates on Nvidia leadership investigations and potential chip export restrictions
analysis.caveats: The source article covers a wide digest of technology news, meaning these global policy shifts may or may not translate directly into immediate US legislation.

events.headline: Director-General: Leverage trade and partnerships to build a resilient ocean economy

items.title: Director-General: Leverage trade and partnerships to build a resilient ocean economy
items.summary: The multilateral trading system provides important tools for the development of a healthy and prosperous ocean economy, Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala said in her keynote speech at an event on Trade, Biodiversity and the Ocean Economy: Pathways to Resilience at the WTO on 5 November. Highlighting the importance of strengthening support for coastal and island economies, she said: Trade is part of the answer. The oceans are an asset of the global commons that can best be managed through multilateral approaches. The event was co-organized by Belgium, Fiji and Portugal.

events.article_text:
The ocean is both a vital natural asset and a major source of trade, food security and livelihoods, DG Okonjo-Iweala said, noting that the ocean economy is valued at US$ 2.6 trillion and supports around 133 million jobs, while more than 80% of globally traded goods travel by sea. When it comes to the ocean economy, "there is no trade-off. . If we are to be prosperous, we must be sustainable," the Director-General said, warning that the decline in marine biodiversity threatens the trade, food security and livelihoods that depend on it.

The Director-General pointed out that, despite current geopolitical turbulence, 72 per cent of world goods trade still takes place on WTO most-favoured-nation terms. She stressed that the multilateral trading system has delivered for sustainable ocean development, notably through the WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies. The Agreement, which entered into force in September 2025, is the first WTO agreement with environmental sustainability at its core. It prohibits subsidies to illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, fishing of overfished stocks, and fishing on the unregulated high seas.

She urged members to complete the remaining negotiations on fisheries subsidies, known as "Fish 2", which would further enhance the disciplines of the Agreement, she said.

DG Okonjo-Iweala also pointed to the importance of helping island and coastal economies move up the value chain in the ocean economy by improving access to technology, skills, infrastructure and finance needed to process products, obtain certification and reach markets.

"Trade already offers tools" for the development of the ocean economy, she said. These include the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement, which supports rapid cross-border trade of perishable goods; the WTO Dialogue on Plastics Pollution, which is looking into issues such as single-use plastics and access to waste-management technologies; discussions on environmental sustainability and access to goods and services needed for the green transition; and development initiatives such as the Enhanced Integrated Framework and the Standards and Trade Development Facility.

The Director-General highlighted the importance of partnerships for the sustainable development of the ocean economy, such as the Geneva Nexus, an informal knowledge-sharing group established by the Permanent Mission of Portugal and a number of other Missions to the United Nations in Geneva in June 2026. This initiative is focused on addressing issues of ocean governance, trade, biodiversity, health and food security. The organizers have organized sessions with a number of international organizations, namely the World Health Organization (WHO), the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the WTO, United Nations Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF).

Looking ahead, DG Okonjo-Iweala called on partners to step up efforts and strengthen cooperation, bringing together the various resources available in Geneva and translating connections into action. "We have the instruments. We need to do more. Let's work together and deliver," she concluded.

The DG's speech was followed by a panel discussion with experts from partner organizations of the Geneva Nexus, moderated by Yuvan Beejadhur, Senior Advisor to the Director-General of the WTO.

Problems viewing this page? If so, please contact [email protected] giving details of the operating system and web browser you are using.

analysis.tldr: Global pushes to protect ocean health and fishing rules could eventually reshape trade costs and food prices for everyday shoppers.
the_story: World Trade Organization Director-General Okonjo-Iweala stated that the global ocean economy is valued at US$ 2.6 trillion and supports 133 million jobs, with over 80% of traded goods moving by sea.

She highlighted that the WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies entered into force in September 2025 to ban harmful funding for illegal and overfished practices, while urging members to finish 'Fish 2' negotiations.
She noted tools like the Trade Facilitation Agreement that help speed up cross-border trade for perishable goods, alongside ongoing work on plastics pollution and green transitions.
analysis.what_happened: WTO Director-General Okonjo-Iweala gave a speech urging countries to use trade rules and partnerships to protect ocean resources. She pointed out that declining marine life threatens global food security and livelihoods, and highlighted existing agreements designed to curb harmful fishing subsidies.
analysis.analogy: It is like a town council setting strict rules on who can fish in the local lake so that the fish do not run out, rather than letting everyone overfish until the water is empty.
why_it_matters_india: Strict international fishing rules could alter catch limits and operational costs for commercial fishing sectors.
Efforts to streamline perishable goods transport could eventually touch seafood and agricultural exports from coastal nations like India.
Global trade regulations on marine safety and plastics filter down into supply chain compliance for Indian exporters.
Changes in international food security policies indirectly influence domestic food and commodity price trends.

impacts.target: Seafood export compliance costs for Indian companies
impacts.rationale: Stricter global sustainability and certification requirements mean businesses spend more to prove compliance, which can squeeze smaller exporters.
If curbs on fishing or shipping raise the cost of seafood and marine transport, grocery bills could edge higher for households.

watch_next: Progress on the 'Fish 2' fisheries subsidy negotiations at the WTO
Updates on international rules regarding plastics pollution and maritime shipping
analysis.caveats: This article is based entirely on a speech about broad policy goals rather than a legally binding trade restriction taking immediate effect today.

history.title: A speech that cost India 20% of its currency
history.where: United States, felt hardest in India
history.what: Fed chairman Ben Bernanke suggested in testimony that the Fed might slow its bond buying "in the next few meetings". He did not change any policy. Within four months the rupee had fallen from 55 to 68 per dollar and India was labelled one of the "Fragile Five".
history.why: Years of near-zero US rates had pushed investors into emerging markets hunting for yield. India ran a large current account deficit — importing far more than it exported, with gold and oil the biggest items — and was therefore dependent on that foreign money continuing to arrive. The hint that the tide might turn was enough; no actual policy change was needed.
history.impact: The rupee fell about 20% in four months. Indian bond yields spiked, the stock market fell sharply, and the RBI raised rates into an already slowing economy to defend the currency.
history.policy: The RBI opened a special concessional window to attract dollar deposits from Indians abroad, raising about $34 billion. Gold import duties were raised steeply to curb the import bill. And in 2016 India adopted a formal inflation-targeting framework, which addressed the underlying cause.
history.consequence: India's current account deficit narrowed sharply and reserves were rebuilt to levels that made the 2018 and 2022 dollar shocks far less painful. The gold import duty also created a large smuggling industry — an unintended consequence that took years to unwind.
history.pattern: An economy dependent on foreign capital is hostage to a foreign central bank's tone, not just its decisions. The vulnerability is built during the good years, when the money is arriving and nobody asks why.
history.india_echo: This is the single clearest lesson for an Indian investor about why the Fed matters here. Nothing changed in India that summer. The Nifty fell anyway, because the marginal buyer of Indian shares sits in New York.
history.watch_for: India's current account deficit as a share of GDP, and the share of the market owned by foreign investors. Together they size the exposure.
